meta.abstract: Vistra Corp (VST, NYSE) is the Irving, Texas-headquartered integrated retail electricity and power generation company that emerged from the post-bankruptcy reorganisation of Texas Competitive Electric Holdings (a subsidiary of Energy Future Holdings) in October 2016 and was subsequently consolidated through the 2018 acquisition of Dynegy and the 2024 acquisition of Energy Harbor's nuclear and competitive power assets. CEO Jim Burke was named to the role in August 2022, succeeding Curt Morgan; Burke's prior role was Chief Operating Officer. The Energy Harbor acquisition in March 2024 for approximately $3.4 billion was the most consequential single transaction of the post-2022 period, adding approximately 4 gigawatts of PJM nuclear capacity and substantially expanding Vistra's contracted-revenue and PJM-capacity-market exposure. The retail electricity business under the TXU Energy and adjacent brand portfolio serves approximately 5 million customers across multiple deregulated US markets. Fiscal year 2025 (calendar year 2025) produced adjusted EBITDA in the approximate $5.5-6.5 billion range and adjusted free cash flow in the $3-4 billion range; revenue was in the $20+ billion range reflecting both the wholesale generation and the retail electricity supply businesses. The board is chaired by Scott Helm with directors carrying utility-industry, finance, and broader operational experience. The investment proposition compresses AI data centre electricity demand sustainability, the structural exposure to both ERCOT and PJM markets (geographic diversification beyond pure PJM nuclear peers like Talen and beyond pure ERCOT-anchored peers), the nuclear fleet positioning for hyperscaler PPAs (parallel to the Constellation Microsoft TMI and Talen Amazon Susquehanna transactions), and the integrated retail-wholesale business model that provides natural hedging across the wholesale-electricity-price cycle.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
In May 2024, Vistra Corp signed a multi-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft for nuclear capacity from its 2,400-megawatt Comanche Peak plant in Glen Rose, Texas — the first major hyperscaler-nuclear PPA at scale among US merchant generators, executed approximately four months before Constellation Energy's September 2024 agreement with Microsoft for capacity from Three Mile Island Unit 1. That sequence placed Vistra ahead of the field in what became the defining structural theme in US power markets: the alignment of always-on nuclear baseload with the round-the-clock consumption profiles of AI data-centre operators. Within eighteen months, the company signed two further hyperscaler agreements covering a combined 3,800 megawatts, transforming what had been a single transaction into a systematic PPA strategy spanning both the Texas and PJM markets.

Vistra Corp ([VST, NYSE](https://investor.vistracorp.com/financial-information)) is headquartered in Irving, Texas, and as of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026 carries a market capitalisation of approximately $52.7 billion. Jim Burke has served as President and Chief Executive Officer since 1 August 2022; Kristopher Moldovan has served as Chief Financial Officer since 2022.

## Origin: Out of the Energy Future Holdings Estate

The company traces its lineage to the October 2016 emergence of Texas Competitive Electric Holdings — the unregulated generation and retail arm of Energy Future Holdings — from Chapter 11 bankruptcy. EFH had been created in the 2007 leveraged buyout of TXU Corporation by KKR, TPG, and Goldman Sachs, a $45 billion transaction that subsequently buckled as shale gas fundamentally re-priced the competitive generation stack. The post-reorganisation entity took the Vistra Energy name, retained the TXU Energy retail brand, and migrated to NYSE listing in 2017. Burke's trajectory within the group — CEO of TXU Energy, then COO of Vistra, then President and CEO — reflected the company's integrated retail-plus-generation identity. Vistra, as of the snapshot date, was the largest US competitive power generator by installed capacity — approximately 41 gigawatts across nuclear, gas, coal, solar, and battery storage — and the largest US competitive retail electricity provider, serving roughly 5 million customers principally through TXU Energy in Texas.

## The Energy Harbor Transformation

Vistra announced the acquisition of Energy Harbor Corp on 6 March 2023 and closed the transaction on 1 March 2024 for total consideration of approximately $3.43 billion: roughly $3.0 billion in cash, assumption of approximately $430 million in Energy Harbor debt, and a 15 percent equity stake in Vistra Vision — the Vistra subsidiary housing the combined nuclear and renewables portfolio — transferred to Energy Harbor's prior stakeholders. The deal added four nuclear reactors: Davis-Besse (Ohio), Perry (Ohio), and Beaver Valley Units 1 and 2 (Pennsylvania), totalling approximately 4,000 megawatts, expanding Vistra's nuclear fleet from the single 2,400-megawatt Comanche Peak plant to a 6.4-gigawatt, five-plant portfolio spanning Texas, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. Roughly one million retail customers in PJM markets accompanied the transaction. The acquisition was among the first significant US merchant-nuclear M&A events executed in the post-Inflation Reduction Act environment, where [Section 45U production tax credits](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001692819) establish an earnings floor that transformed previously distressed plants into durable cash-generating infrastructure.

## The Hyperscaler PPA Cascade

The May 2024 Microsoft Comanche Peak agreement proved the opening move in a series. In September 2025, [Vistra disclosed](https://www.investing.com/news/sec-filings/vistra-signs-20year-power-purchase-agreement-for-1200-mw-of-nuclear-power-93CH-4260635) a second 20-year PPA for 1,200 megawatts from Comanche Peak, with Amazon Web Services as counterparty, delivery commencing in the fourth quarter of 2027 and ramping to full capacity by 2032. Vistra estimated the contract could add 8–10 percent of incremental adjusted free cash flow before growth at full utilisation. In January 2026, the company announced a 20-year agreement with Meta for 2,609 megawatts — [2,176 megawatts of operating capacity from Perry and Davis-Besse in Ohio and Beaver Valley in Pennsylvania, plus 433 megawatts from uprates at those three plants](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/vistra-and-meta-announce-agreements-to-support-nuclear-plants-in-pjm-and-add-new-nuclear-generation-to-the-grid-302656941.html), constituting the largest nuclear uprates supported by a single corporate customer in US history.

> "This commitment from Meta provides Vistra the certainty needed to invest in these plants and communities and bring new nuclear generation online for the grid." — Jim Burke, January 2026

## Financial Re-Rating

The earnings trajectory captures the structural shift. Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA rose from $3.6 billion in fiscal 2023 to approximately $5.7 billion in fiscal 2024, driven by the first full year of Energy Harbor contribution, ERCOT capacity scarcity dynamics, and elevated PJM capacity market clearing prices from the 2025–2026 auction cycle.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Adj. EBITDA (Ongoing Ops.) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | $14.8B | $3.6B | [Vistra IR](https://investor.vistracorp.com/financial-information) |
| 2024 | $17.2B | $5.7B | [PR Newswire, Feb 2025](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/vistra-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-results-302387102.html) |
| 2025 | $17.7B | $5.9B | [PR Newswire, Feb 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/vistra-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results-302697962.html) |

> "I am proud of the 2025 performance of our Vistra team — this was truly a transformational year for our company." — Jim Burke, February 2026

Management guided fiscal 2026 Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA of $6.8 billion to $7.6 billion, predicated on continued capacity price strength in both ERCOT and PJM and the progressive layering of hyperscaler PPA revenues onto the nuclear fleet.

## Moss Landing: Battery Storage in the Dock

On 16 January 2025, a fire broke out at Vistra's 350-megawatt Moss Landing lithium-ion battery energy storage facility in Monterey County, California — then among the largest such installations globally. A failed fire suppression system within a battery rack allowed the blaze to spread; the facility reignited on 18 February from batteries buried beneath rubble, prompting further evacuations of nearby residents. Vistra transferred the asset to its Asset Closure segment and disclosed that [business interruption insurance proceeds and environmental remediation expenses were ongoing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm). The California Public Utilities Commission's independent root-cause analysis remained active as of the snapshot date; return-to-service planning targeted mid-2026 contingent on investigation completion. [Multiple civil lawsuits against Vistra and PG&E](https://localnewsmatters.org/2025/05/22/wave-of-litigation-follows-january-fire-at-vistra-moss-landing-battery-facility/) had been filed within months of the initial incident.

The fire raised systemic questions about lithium-ion battery safety at utility scale in densely populated coastal locations — questions that Vistra's nuclear and gas acquisitions had not posed.

## Central Questions

At the snapshot date, Vistra traded as the principal Texas-anchored US merchant power franchise with deepening and diversified AI-data-centre exposure across its nuclear fleet — Microsoft, AWS, and Meta having contracted a combined total of approximately 5,000-plus megawatts of nuclear capacity from assets in Texas, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. Three questions frame the analysis ahead. First, having demonstrated the ability to close hyperscaler PPAs across the Comanche Peak and PJM nuclear assets, can Vistra extend that framework to its substantial gas fleet, and what incremental premium might carbon-intensity considerations impose? Second, following the Calpine acquisition that created a larger scaled competitor, how does Vistra position its combined 41-gigawatt franchise against a pro-forma Constellation with deeper PJM nuclear depth and a competing hyperscaler-PPA pipeline? Third, what does the Moss Landing incident — and the litigation and remediation tail it carries — signal about the velocity and risk tolerance of the company's battery storage ambitions against the backdrop of a nuclear and gas cash-generation engine that funds everything else?

chapters.title: From Energy Future Holdings Chapter 11 to the Energy Harbor acquisition
chapters.body:
## The integrated utility and the leveraged bet

Before the private-equity era, TXU Corporation was the defining integrated electric utility of deregulated Texas — a sprawling holding company that combined rate-regulated wires assets, merchant generation, and the state's largest retail electricity franchise. Its competitive generation arm, weighted heavily toward coal-fired baseload capacity in ERCOT, operated under the logic that Texas population growth would drive sustained power demand and that whoever owned the baseload plant would capture the price upside.

In October 2007, that thesis attracted what was then the largest leveraged buyout in history. A consortium led by KKR and TPG Capital, with Goldman Sachs' private equity arm as a significant co-investor, acquired TXU Corporation for approximately $44 billion — a transaction that loaded the surviving entity, renamed Energy Future Holdings, with roughly $40 billion of debt. EFH was reorganised into three principal subsidiaries: Texas Competitive Electric Holdings (TCEH), which held the competitive generation fleet and TXU Energy retail; Luminant, the generation operating company; and Oncor Electric Delivery, the regulated transmission and distribution utility.

The financial bet was directional: natural gas prices would remain elevated or rise, preserving the implied margin for coal-fired generation that was priced against gas at the margin in ERCOT. It was, in retrospect, one of the more expensive single-variable errors in private-equity history.

## The shale revolution and the Chapter 11

The Barnett Shale had already begun producing in volume when the EFH deal closed. By 2009 the Haynesville and Marcellus plays were flooding the US gas market with supply that permanently restructured the price curve. Henry Hub spot prices, which had spiked above $13 per MMBtu in mid-2008, collapsed below $2 by April 2012. In ERCOT — a power market that sets its marginal price against gas-fired generation — lower gas prices meant lower wholesale electricity prices, which meant structurally impaired merchant margins for Luminant's coal-heavy fleet.

Energy Future Holdings, carrying its LBO debt load against a deteriorating margin environment, entered creditor restructuring negotiations in 2013. In April 2014 the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware — at the time one of the largest corporate bankruptcies in US history by debt quantum. The filing separated EFH's regulated and competitive businesses along structural lines embedded in the original acquisition architecture. Oncor Electric Delivery, ring-fenced from the competitive businesses, proceeded through a separate sales process that ultimately brought the regulated T&D asset to Sempra Energy. TCEH — the competitive generation and retail vehicle — pursued its own reorganisation track.

## The birth of Vistra Energy

In October 2016, TCEH emerged from bankruptcy as a standalone competitive generation and retail company, renamed Vistra Energy. TCEH's senior secured creditors received equity in the newly-formed entity as their reorganisation recovery — a structure that delivered a disciplined capital table to the post-bankruptcy vehicle, unburdened by the debt architecture that had sunk EFH. Vistra Energy initially traded over-the-counter before graduating to the New York Stock Exchange in 2017 under the ticker VST.

What emerged was a merchant power pure-play: Vistra retained the Luminant generation brand across coal, gas, and nuclear assets in ERCOT; the TXU Energy retail brand, which was the largest competitive retail electricity provider in Texas; and, critically, Comanche Peak — the two-unit, 2.4-gigawatt pressurised-water nuclear plant in Somervell County, Texas, that would later anchor the first major hyperscaler-nuclear PPA in the United States. The post-bankruptcy management team, led by Chief Executive Curt Morgan, moved quickly to establish Vistra as a disciplined capital allocator: debt was retired, share buybacks were executed, and the operational focus shifted to free cash flow from the existing fleet.

## The Dynegy acquisition and the PJM foothold

In April 2018, Vistra completed the acquisition of Dynegy — a rival competitive power generator with a multi-regional fleet spanning PJM, MISO, ISO-NE, and NYISO — in an all-stock transaction that valued Dynegy's equity at approximately $1.7 billion, with Vistra assuming Dynegy's outstanding debt in addition. The combined company cleared approximately 38 gigawatts of generation capacity, roughly doubling Vistra's footprint and diversifying it across five regional transmission organisations.

The strategic logic was consolidation at distressed valuations. Vistra at emergence was ERCOT-concentrated with limited presence outside Texas; Dynegy brought PJM and MISO capacity — gas-fired combined-cycle and peaker plants, plus legacy coal assets undergoing retirement — that established Vistra as a multi-regional merchant operator. The Dynegy integration also established the template for the subsequent Energy Harbor transaction: acquire a creditor-controlled competitive generation asset at a price set through restructuring process rather than a contested strategic auction, absorb the operational and commercial infrastructure, and generate synergies from procurement, commercial optimisation, and capital structure rationalisation.

## The Burke succession and the IRA tailwind

In August 2022, Curt Morgan retired as Chief Executive after leading Vistra through post-bankruptcy emergence, the Dynegy integration, and the extraordinary market conditions of Winter Storm Uri in February 2021. James A. Burke — who had served as Chief Operating Officer and had earlier led TXU Energy as its Chief Executive — succeeded him on 1 August 2022.

The timing was consequential. Seventeen days later, President Biden signed the Inflation Reduction Act into law on 16 August 2022. The IRA's Section 45U Production Tax Credit established a zero-emissions electricity production credit for existing nuclear generation, creating a floor price mechanism that materially improved the forward cash flow profile of Vistra's Comanche Peak asset. For merchant nuclear operators running fully dispatchable, high-capacity-factor generation, the 45U PTC converted a portion of nuclear value from market-price exposure to an indexed federal credit, reducing cash flow volatility and sharpening the investment thesis for fleet expansion.

Burke's strategic thesis — nuclear as the backbone of grid reliability and AI data centre power supply — was already visible in Vistra's capital allocation before the Energy Harbor announcement.

## Energy Harbor: The nuclear transformation

On 6 March 2023, Vistra announced the acquisition of Energy Harbor Corporation — a competitive nuclear and retail power company formed from the 2020 bankruptcy reorganisation of FirstEnergy Solutions — for total consideration of approximately $3.43 billion. The deal structure combined approximately $3.0 billion in cash, assumption of approximately $430 million of Energy Harbor debt, and a 15% equity stake in a newly-created Vistra subsidiary, Vistra Vision, which would consolidate the acquired Energy Harbor nuclear assets alongside the existing Comanche Peak plant and Vistra's broader renewables and storage portfolio.

The four reactors acquired were Davis-Besse (a single-unit boiling-water reactor in Ottawa County, Ohio), Perry (a single-unit boiling-water reactor in Lake County, Ohio), and Beaver Valley Units 1 and 2 (pressurised-water reactors in Beaver County, Pennsylvania) — together adding approximately 4,000 megawatts of PJM nuclear capacity. The acquisition transferred approximately one million retail electricity customers in PJM competitive markets alongside the four reactors, meaningfully expanding Vistra's retail franchise outside Texas.

Burke, announcing the transaction in March 2023, described it as transformative — establishing Vistra as the nation's largest competitive power producer and positioning the company as the second-largest operator of nuclear capacity in the United States. Kristopher Moldovan, Vistra's Chief Financial Officer, characterised the deal's financial structure as capital-efficient given the 45U PTC floor and the PJM capacity market pricing environment. The transaction closed on 1 March 2024, following Nuclear Regulatory Commission and Federal Trade Commission clearances.

The Energy Harbor close transformed Vistra's nuclear positioning from a single 2.4-gigawatt Texas plant to a 6.4-gigawatt fleet spanning three states. Within PJM — where the July 2024 capacity auction cleared at prices that surprised even bullish market participants, reflecting structural capacity scarcity across the region — the four Energy Harbor reactors commanded premium values in both energy and capacity markets.

## What the post-bankruptcy era produced

Across eight years from the October 2016 emergence, Vistra's evolution followed a consistent arc: bankruptcy reorganisation delivered a disciplined capital structure; the Dynegy acquisition added multi-regional scale; the IRA reshaped the nuclear economics; and Energy Harbor transformed a Texas-focused merchant generator into the largest competitive power producer in the United States by installed capacity.

| Metric | FY 2022 | FY 2023 | FY 2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue (USD bn) | 13.7 | 14.8 | 17.2 |
| Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) | 3.1 | 3.6 | 5.7 |
| Nuclear capacity (GW) | 2.4 | 2.4 | 6.4 |
| Total generation capacity (GW, approx.) | ~38 | ~38 | ~41 |

Vistra exited 2024 as a ~41-gigawatt operator carrying 6.4 gigawatts of nuclear capacity, approximately five million retail customers across deregulated US markets, a signed Microsoft PPA for Comanche Peak output, and a management team publicly signalling further hyperscaler PPA discussions across the expanded nuclear fleet. The trajectory from TCEH creditor recovery vehicle to principal Texas-anchored AI power play was, by any measure, among the more improbable reinventions in the history of US competitive electricity.

chapters.title: Generation by region, TXU retail, and the Vistra Vision subsidiary
chapters.body:
## Five Regional Footprints, One Retail Anchor

When Vistra Corp filed its 2024 annual report with the Securities and Exchange Commission, it described itself as the largest competitive power generator in the United States by installed capacity — a claim that would have been inconceivable eight years earlier, when the company emerged from the Energy Future Holdings Chapter 11 as a rebranded Texas generator with one nuclear plant and a politically embattled coal portfolio. By the close of fiscal 2024, the company was reporting approximately $17.2 billion in revenue and approximately $5.7 billion in adjusted EBITDA, a scale achieved through a combination of organic ERCOT market repricing and the transformative March 2024 acquisition of Energy Harbor. The operating structure that produced those numbers was organised across five regional wholesale markets — ERCOT, PJM, MISO, NYISO, and ISO-NE — plus the TXU Energy retail franchise and a newly created subsidiary called Vistra Vision.

## ERCOT: The Texas Foundation

Texas remained the largest single region in Vistra's portfolio, and ERCOT's structural characteristics made it the most consequential one for earnings trajectory. Vistra's Texas footprint centred on the 2.4 GW Comanche Peak nuclear station in Glen Rose — two units, Unit 1 and Unit 2, operating at consistently high capacity factors — supplemented by a substantial fleet of natural gas combined-cycle plants and peaking units distributed across ERCOT's four weather zones.

ERCOT's design as an energy-only market, without a centralised capacity mechanism of the type used in PJM, meant that scarcity pricing events — when system-wide supply margins tightened and the nodal price approached or reached the market cap — could generate disproportionate revenue in short, concentrated intervals. The operating reserve demand curve, which Vistra's executives frequently referenced in earnings discussions as a structural feature favouring dispatchable generation, served to monetise capacity scarcity directly into energy prices rather than through a separate auction. Texas's emergence as the preferred landing zone for US AI data centre development — driven by low land costs, proximity to large power infrastructure, and a permitting environment markedly faster than northeastern and Pacific states — strained ERCOT load forecasts materially through 2024 and into 2025, with the Electric Reliability Council of Texas revising its interconnection queue demand estimates upward multiple times over the period.

Comanche Peak sat at the centre of Vistra's commercial strategy in ERCOT. As a baseload nuclear plant qualified for the IRA Section 45U production tax credit, Comanche Peak's economics carried a government-provided floor. The May 2024 Microsoft PPA (see Snapshot) layered contracted revenue atop that floor while preserving merchant upside on uncontracted output.

## PJM: The Energy Harbor Transformation

Prior to the March 2024 Energy Harbor close (see Corporate History for deal terms), Vistra's PJM footprint was modest. The acquisition added approximately 4,000 MW of dispatchable zero-carbon baseload capacity, bringing total nuclear to approximately 6.4 GW across five plants. The July 2024 PJM capacity auction, clearing at approximately $269/MW-day — well above prior levels — meant the four acquired reactors captured elevated capacity revenues immediately.

| Nuclear asset | Location | Approximate capacity | ISO/RTO |
|---|---|---|---|
| Comanche Peak Unit 1 & 2 | Glen Rose, TX | 2,400 MW | ERCOT |
| Davis-Besse | Oak Harbor, OH | ~908 MW | PJM |
| Perry | North Perry, OH | ~1,240 MW | PJM |
| Beaver Valley Unit 1 | Shippingport, PA | ~895 MW | PJM |
| Beaver Valley Unit 2 | Shippingport, PA | ~895 MW | PJM |
| **Total nuclear** | | **~6,338 MW** | |

*Sources: Vistra Corp 2024 10-K, [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001692819](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001692819)*

Energy Harbor also brought approximately one million retail customers in PJM-overlapping competitive retail markets, broadening Vistra's retail presence beyond Texas for the first time at material scale.

## MISO, NYISO, and ISO-NE: Secondary Positions

Outside of ERCOT and PJM, Vistra operated natural gas and, in diminishing quantities, coal-fired assets across the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO), the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), and ISO New England (ISO-NE). These three regions collectively represented a smaller share of total segment contribution than ERCOT or PJM, and the company's coal fleet across MISO in particular was subject to an active retirement schedule — reflecting the combined pressure of age, tightening environmental compliance costs, and natural gas and renewable economics that persistently undercut economic dispatch. Vistra's strategy in the secondary regions leaned toward holding dispatchable gas assets where capacity market participation or ancillary service revenues justified continued operation, while systematically exiting coal positions where the retirement economics were more attractive than continued operation.

## TXU Energy and the Retail Franchise

TXU Energy, the retail electricity brand Vistra inherited from the TCEH bankruptcy estate, served approximately five million residential and business customers across the Texas competitive retail electricity market by the close of 2024. Texas's deregulated electricity market — covering roughly 85% of the state's load and served by competitive retail providers operating over a common distribution infrastructure — had been Vistra's largest single source of operating cash flow contribution for most of its post-bankruptcy history. The retail business functioned as a natural hedge against the wholesale generation portfolio: when ERCOT wholesale prices rose sharply on scarcity events, the generation segment captured premium revenues, while the retail segment faced cost pressure unless pass-through mechanisms or fixed-price contract mixes absorbed the increase.

Vistra supplemented TXU Energy's primarily Texas-residential focus with Ambit Energy, a multi-state direct-sales retail brand acquired in 2019, and additional competitive retail brands serving commercial and industrial customers in deregulated markets beyond Texas. The combined retail customer count, inclusive of the PJM-region customers added through Energy Harbor, positioned Vistra as the largest competitive retail electricity provider in the United States by customer count.

The retail business carried a structurally different financial profile than the generation segment: relatively capital-light, operationally intensive at the customer acquisition and billing layer, and sensitive to customer churn rates and the competitive dynamics of a Texas retail market where hundreds of licensed providers competed on price comparison platforms. Management historically characterised the retail franchise as a strategic anchor — its predictable cash flows offsetting the earnings volatility inherent in merchant generation — rather than a high-growth vehicle.

## Vistra Vision: The Nuclear-and-Clean Subsidiary

The March 2024 Energy Harbor acquisition gave rise to a new entity in Vistra's corporate structure: Vistra Vision, a wholly-owned Vistra subsidiary — or more precisely, 85% Vistra-owned — that was designated to hold the combined nuclear fleet (Comanche Peak plus the four Energy Harbor reactors), the renewables portfolio, and the battery storage assets. The 15% minority interest in Vistra Vision was held by Energy Harbor's former stakeholders, received as part of the deal consideration in lieu of additional cash.

Vistra Vision served multiple strategic purposes. As a distinct legal vehicle holding the zero-carbon generation assets, it created optionality for future capital market transactions — a partial IPO, a minority stake sale, or a capital raise at the subsidiary level — without requiring a restructuring of the parent company. The subsidiary also concentrated the IRA Section 45U nuclear production tax credit-eligible capacity in a single entity, simplifying the tracking and allocation of those credits across the fleet.

## Battery Storage: DeCordova and the Vistra Vision Portfolio

Vistra Vision's portfolio extended beyond nuclear to encompass the company's growing battery storage footprint. The 260 MW DeCordova battery energy storage system in Texas — co-located with a legacy generation site near Fort Worth — was among the larger standalone battery installations in ERCOT and participated in ancillary service markets alongside the energy market. The January 2025 fire at the 350 MW Moss Landing facility in California (see Snapshot) added an unplanned variable to the storage segment's contribution projections for fiscal 2025.

## Segment Revenue Profile

Vistra reported consolidated revenue of approximately $17.2 billion in fiscal 2024, against $14.8 billion in 2023 and $13.7 billion in 2022. The step-up from 2023 to 2024 reflected both the full-year addition of Energy Harbor's revenue streams — the acquisition closed on March 1, meaning fiscal 2024 captured approximately ten months of Energy Harbor contribution — and continued ERCOT wholesale price uplift.

| Fiscal year | Revenue (USD bn) | Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | $13.7 | $3.1 |
| 2023 | $14.8 | $3.6 |
| 2024 | $17.2 | $5.7 |

*Sources: Vistra Corp 10-K filings, [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001692819](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001692819)*

The adjusted EBITDA expansion from $3.6 billion in 2023 to $5.7 billion in 2024 — a $2.1 billion year-on-year increase, or roughly 58% growth — reflected the combined effect of Energy Harbor's nuclear contribution, the elevated PJM capacity auction clearing, the IRA production tax credit economics on the nuclear fleet, and the Comanche Peak Microsoft PPA revenue. Together, those four factors compressed the earnings multiple the market had historically assigned to a merchant power generator and began to justify the valuation re-rating that made Vistra one of the best-performing large-cap US equities across the 2024–2025 period.

chapters.title: $17.2B revenue, $5.7B adjusted EBITDA, and the Energy Harbor accretion
chapters.body:
## The 2024 Earnings Step-Change

Vistra Corp closed fiscal year 2024 with revenue of $17.2 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $5.7 billion — figures that marked the most consequential earnings inflection in the company's post-bankruptcy history. The adjusted EBITDA figure represented a 58 percent expansion over the $3.6 billion recorded in fiscal 2023, and nearly doubled the $3.1 billion produced in 2022. Three forces converged to generate that step-change: the March 2024 close of the Energy Harbor acquisition, structural capacity scarcity in ERCOT, and a broad repricing of PJM capacity market revenues that the company's newly enlarged nuclear fleet was positioned to capture in full.

The revenue trajectory over the three-year window told a story of compounding scale. Vistra moved from $13.7 billion in 2022 to $14.8 billion in 2023, a gain that reflected organic ERCOT tightening and incremental retail growth, before the $17.2 billion 2024 total absorbed nine months of Energy Harbor's contribution. The company entered 2025 with a materially different earnings base than the one Jim Burke inherited when he assumed the CEO role in August 2022 — a fleet of approximately 41 gigawatts spanning nuclear, gas, coal retirement, and growing storage, anchored by the only scaled nuclear portfolio straddling both ERCOT and PJM.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) | EBITDA Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 13.7 | 3.1 | 22.6% |
| 2023 | 14.8 | 3.6 | 24.3% |
| 2024 | 17.2 | 5.7 | 33.1% |

## The Energy Harbor Accretion Engine

The financial arithmetic of the Energy Harbor acquisition (see Corporate History for deal terms) became clearer in the twelve months following the March 2024 close. The Vistra Vision structure ringfenced nuclear and clean energy assets into a subsidiary with an external 15% equity stake, creating a vehicle through which the consideration was partly paid in units of a premium-valued clean-energy entity. This structure reflected a bilateral view that the nuclear fleet — valued with IRA Section 45U tailwinds and AI-cycle optionality — warranted a separate enterprise valuation distinct from Vistra's merchant gas and retail operations.

## Section 45U and the Nuclear Earnings Floor

The IRA's Section 45U production tax credit provides a per-megawatt-hour subsidy for zero-emission nuclear generation that phases down as wholesale prices rise but establishes an effective floor when prices fall. At a 95 percent capacity factor, the 6.4 GW portfolio generates approximately 53 terawatt-hours annually. The structural effect is an earnings floor that did not exist pre-IRA: in low-price environments, the credit compensates; in high-price environments, the full upside flows to EBITDA. The company's disclosures increasingly treat the nuclear fleet as a de facto baseload annuity.

## PJM Capacity Market Repricing

The July 2024 PJM capacity auction for the 2025-2026 delivery year cleared at prices exceeding $269 per megawatt-day — a dramatic repricing from the deeply suppressed levels that had characterised PJM capacity markets for much of the prior decade. The auction reflected a fundamental reassessment of capacity adequacy across the PJM footprint, driven by accelerating data centre load growth across Virginia and adjacent zones, coal and gas plant retirements outpacing replacement, and structural tightening that PJM's own capacity adequacy analyses had flagged as approaching critical in the late 2020s.

For Vistra, the PJM repricing translated into substantial incremental capacity revenue for the Energy Harbor reactors — revenue streams that were largely absent from the pre-acquisition Vistra financial model, which was almost entirely ERCOT-anchored. The four Energy Harbor units operate as must-run baseload capacity within the PJM footprint, qualifying for the full clearing price on their offered capacity. At $269/MW-day applied across approximately 4,000 MW of nuclear capacity, the order-of-magnitude annualised capacity revenue contribution runs to several hundred million dollars — a figure that, combined with the energy revenue from elevated wholesale prices, materially explains the Energy Harbor accretion in the 2024 adjusted EBITDA.

The PJM repricing also illustrated the structural asymmetry in Vistra's post-acquisition positioning. Where Vistra pre-2024 was principally exposed to ERCOT energy market dynamics — highly volatile, capacity-market-light, and acutely sensitive to Texas weather patterns — the Energy Harbor acquisition diversified that exposure into PJM's structured capacity framework, where multi-year clearing prices provide more visible forward earnings than ERCOT's energy-only construct.

## ERCOT Scarcity and the AI Data Centre Premium

Vistra's ERCOT footprint remained the engine of the gas-and-retail earnings stack through 2024. ERCOT's operating reserve demand curve — the market mechanism that ramps energy prices toward the $5,000 per megawatt-hour systemwide offer cap as operating reserves thin — produced elevated prices during periods of demand stress, particularly during summer 2024 peak load events.

The structural driver beneath those episodic scarcity events was the accelerating build-out of AI data centre capacity in North Texas. The Dallas-Fort Worth corridor had emerged as the largest US market for hyperscaler computing investment by square footage, driven by a combination of permissive interconnection timelines, an available labour pool, and the commercial attractiveness of Texas's competitive power market. ERCOT's own load forecasts, revised upward through 2024, incorporated the data centre demand surge, suggesting that structural tightening — not simply weather-driven variability — would characterise the ERCOT balance through the end of the decade.

Vistra's position within that dynamic was straightforward: as the largest generator by installed capacity in ERCOT, with a gas peaker and combined-cycle fleet capable of capturing scarcity pricing, and with the Comanche Peak nuclear plant operating as an uncorrelated must-run baseload, the company sat at the intersection of two premium pricing regimes simultaneously: scarcity rents during stress events, and the structural load growth that was compressing ERCOT's reserve margins.

## The Microsoft Comanche Peak PPA

The May 2024 Microsoft PPA (see Snapshot for context) converted a portion of Comanche Peak's output into contracted cash flow, accepting some degree of upside cap in exchange for revenue certainty. Management indicated the agreement was viewed as a template for further hyperscaler engagement, with active pipeline discussions across the nuclear fleet.

## Capital Allocation: Buybacks and Debt Management

Vistra's capital allocation through the 2024 earnings cycle reflected the confidence of a management team operating with a materially expanded free cash flow profile. The company maintained an active share repurchase programme — one of the more aggressive return-of-capital postures among US independent power producers — alongside a dividend that was modest in absolute terms relative to the buyback scale. [Vistra 10-K FY2024, Capital Allocation section]

The Energy Harbor financing added to the long-term debt stack, and debt management — balancing the incremental leverage from the acquisition against the expanded EBITDA base — became a focal point of investor communication through 2024. The net leverage trajectory, as adjusted EBITDA expanded toward the $5.7 billion 2024 figure, remained a constructive story: the EBITDA multiple on the acquisition consideration declined as the capacity market and nuclear earnings contributions came through.

## Moss Landing: The Battery Storage Exception

The January 2025 Moss Landing fire (see Snapshot) introduced a discrete variable into the 2024 accretion story. The financial framework centres on insurance recovery, ongoing as of the snapshot date. In the context of $5.7 billion adjusted EBITDA, the battery storage portfolio remained a small earnings contributor — the incident was primarily a reputational and risk-framework event rather than an earnings-material loss.

chapters.title: From the 2022 Burke succession to the 2024 Energy Harbor inflection
chapters.body:
## The Burke Era Begins: August 2022

Burke assumed the CEO role from Curt Morgan on August 1, 2022 (see Corporate History for background). The succession came seventeen days before the IRA was signed into law. His strategic inheritance was substantial: ~38 GW across ERCOT, PJM, MISO, and CAISO, plus ~5 million retail customers — but limited to the single 2.4 GW Comanche Peak nuclear plant. Fiscal 2022 produced $3.1 billion adjusted EBITDA against $13.7 billion revenue.

## The Energy Harbor Announcement: March 2023

The March 2023 announcement (see Corporate History for deal terms) marked the most consequential merchant-power acquisition of the post-IRA era. The Section 45U dynamic provided a revenue floor that de-risked the economics substantially. Fiscal 2023 produced $3.6 billion adjusted EBITDA against $14.8 billion revenue — the market beginning to price IRA clarity, tightening ERCOT margins, and hyperscaler demand at scale.

## Energy Harbor Close and the First Hyperscaler PPA: Q1–Q2 2024

The Energy Harbor acquisition closed March 1, 2024 — transforming Vistra's nuclear fleet from a single plant to a 6.4 GW, six-reactor, three-state platform. The May 2024 Microsoft PPA for Comanche Peak output (see Snapshot) followed within two months, establishing Vistra as the first scaled US merchant nuclear operator to execute a hyperscaler PPA at commercial scale.

## ERCOT Scarcity and PJM Repricing: H2 2024

The second half of 2024 delivered the capacity pricing catalysts. PJM's July 2024 auction cleared at approximately $269/MW-day, translating directly into revenue visibility for Vistra's ~4,000 MW of PJM nuclear. In ERCOT, reserve margin compression produced episodic price spikes that the commercial team captured. Full-year 2024 results confirmed the earnings expansion: $17.2 billion revenue and $5.7 billion adjusted EBITDA — 58% EBITDA growth versus fiscal 2022.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 13.7 | 3.1 |
| 2023 | 14.8 | 3.6 |
| 2024 | 17.2 | 5.7 |

*Source: Vistra Corp investor filings; SEC EDGAR CIK 0001692819*

VST shares, alongside Constellation Energy's CEG, emerged as among the best-performing US large-cap equities of 2024-2025. The re-rating dynamic was principally AI-driven: the equity market revised its long-run power demand assumptions materially upward as hyperscaler capital expenditure guidance from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta indicated data centre build programmes measured in hundreds of billions of dollars over multi-year horizons. Zero-carbon, firm generation capacity — nuclear, in particular — traded at a structural premium within this framework, and Vistra's 6.4 gigawatt nuclear fleet, bracketed by the IRA PTC floor and increasingly collateralised by long-dated hyperscaler offtake, sat at the intersection of every relevant demand vector.

## Moss Landing and the Battery Storage Reassessment: January 2025

The January 2025 Moss Landing fire (see Snapshot) introduced a risk variable not fully priced into the merchant storage thesis. Management's response balanced immediate insurance recovery against broader questions about lithium-ion safety management across the storage fleet.

## The Hyperscaler PPA Pipeline: 2025 and Beyond

Through 2025, the hyperscaler PPA pipeline expanded from the Microsoft Comanche Peak template to an active origination environment. Burke's consistent message was disciplined capital allocation: the Vistra Vision nuclear assets would not be priced below the threshold preserving merchant upside. The IRA Section 45U floor provided downside protection; the hyperscaler demand queue provided commercial leverage. Moldovan emphasised the growing proportion of earnings that was contracted, PTC-protected, or capacity-market-secured.

The earnings story from the August 2022 succession through the first quarter of 2026 is, at its core, the story of a timely strategic bet executed with disciplined capital structure management. Burke inherited a platform built for Texas energy market scale; he extended it into PJM nuclear through the Energy Harbor acquisition, anchored it with the first major hyperscaler nuclear PPA through the Microsoft Comanche Peak agreement, and delivered adjusted EBITDA expansion from $3.1 billion to $5.7 billion in two fiscal years. The AI-cycle re-rating of merchant nuclear was the macro tailwind. The execution — the IRA structuring through Vistra Vision, the PJM capacity auction timing, the hyperscaler PPA origination — was the operating story underneath it.

chapters.title: Burke, Moldovan, the Vistra Vision team, and the post-EFH board
chapters.body:
## The Morgan-to-Burke succession and the arc of operating continuity

On August 1, 2022, James A. Burke was named President and Chief Executive Officer of Vistra Corp, succeeding Curtis Morgan. Morgan had served as founding CEO from the company's emergence from the Energy Future Holdings Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2016 through six years of institutional rebuild: the 2018 Dynegy acquisition that doubled Vistra's generation footprint across PJM, MISO, and New York, the catastrophic stress-test of Winter Storm Uri in February 2021, and the early framing of what would become the most durable power-price re-rating cycle in ERCOT's history. When Morgan stepped back, the board did not recruit externally. It promoted the executive who had spent the preceding six years as COO absorbing the Dynegy integration and running the generation fleet alongside the retail operation — and who, before that, had spent eleven years running the retail business itself.

Burke joined TXU Energy — the competitive retail electricity subsidiary that survived the EFH bankruptcy and became the consumer franchise anchoring Vistra's integrated model — in 2004. By 2005 he was Chairman and Chief Executive of TXU Energy, a role he held for eleven years through the EFH period, the bankruptcy, and the post-emergence restructuring. That retail tenure is the foundation of his institutional authority: TXU Energy serves approximately five million residential and business customers in Texas, competing against dozens of rival retail electric providers in the ERCOT open market, and generates the stable margin that underwrites the company's merchant-generation volatility. Burke understands the retail electricity business at granular depth — customer acquisition economics, churn and lifetime-value modelling, hedging programme design, the regulatory interface with the Public Utility Commission of Texas, and the competitive dynamics of a market where consumers can switch providers online in minutes.

When Vistra emerged from bankruptcy in October 2016, Burke transitioned from TXU Energy CEO to Chief Operating Officer of the parent company, a deliberate broadening move that placed him in direct oversight of the wholesale generation fleet. He held the COO portfolio from 2016 to 2020, absorbing the Dynegy integration and the management of a generation mix that spanned natural gas combined-cycle units, legacy coal assets under a retirement programme, the battery storage build-out, and the two-unit Comanche Peak nuclear facility in Glen Rose, Texas. In 2020 he was elevated to President and Chief Financial Officer — an unusual dual portfolio that combined balance-sheet stewardship with operating authority — before the August 2022 CEO succession.

His educational formation is atypical for a large-cap merchant power CEO: a Bachelor of Arts in Economics and an MBA in Finance from Tulane University, followed by both a CPA certification and a CFA designation — the latter a financial-markets credential more common among investment analysts than industrial operators. He subsequently completed an MIT Nuclear Reactor Technology course, a substantive signal of personal commitment to the nuclear asset category that by 2024 would represent more than a third of Vistra's installed capacity. Burke sits on the board of the Nuclear Energy Institute, Washington's principal nuclear power trade association, and on the Tulane Energy Institute's advisory board.

## Kristopher Moldovan: the CFO as balance-sheet architect

Kristopher Moldovan has been Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer since 2022, though his institutional roots at the company trace to 2006 — a decade before the CIK 0001692819 corporate entity existed. His early career followed an engineering-then-law trajectory: a Bachelor of Science in Engineering from the University of Illinois, followed by a law degree from Duke and practice at Gibson, Dunn and Crutcher and Wildman, Harrold, Allen and Dixon, before an in-house move to what was then a predecessor entity of Vistra, where he joined as Senior Counsel. He subsequently added a finance certificate from SMU's Cox School of Business.

The career arc matters because the CFO's command of structured transactions, credit agreement mechanics, and hedging instrument documentation is built on primary professional formation rather than delegated review. His treasury progression — Assistant Treasurer from 2010 to 2017, then SVP and Treasurer from 2017 to 2022 — gave him direct ownership of the liability side of the balance sheet through the most consequential episodes in the company's post-EFH history. The Energy Harbor financing in 2024 tested that capability at scale: Vistra funded approximately $3.4 billion in cash consideration while absorbing roughly $430 million of Energy Harbor's existing debt and issuing a 15 percent equity stake to Energy Harbor stakeholders — all without triggering a ratings downgrade or a dilutive equity offering. The transaction closed March 1, 2024. On subsequent earnings calls, Moldovan's capital allocation commentary — structured around adjusted EBITDA guidance ranges, free cash flow before growth conversion, and the pace of the share repurchase programme — reflects the treasurer's instinct for cash mechanics that accounting earnings can obscure.

## The C-suite: strategy, law, retail, and public affairs

Stacey Doré holds the title of Executive Vice President, Chief Strategy and Sustainability Officer, and Head of Public Affairs — a portfolio spanning M&A origination, regulatory engagement, external communications, and the ESG reporting function. Her formation is lawyerly: she began at Vinson and Elkins, the Houston firm that has served as institutional counsel to the Texas energy industry for generations, before moving in-house to InfraREIT as SVP and General Counsel and subsequently to Hunt Utility Services and its regulated-transmission subsidiary Sharyland Utilities as CEO. The Sharyland operating experience — a Texas transmission utility serving rural ERCOT territory under regulated cost-of-service economics — is a genuinely different commercial model from Vistra's merchant-generation core and provided rare CEO-level exposure to the infrastructure and regulatory side of the electricity system. Doré sits on the Williams Companies board, providing current exposure to the natural gas midstream sector increasingly entangled with power-market dynamics.

Stephanie Zapata Moore serves as EVP and General Counsel, having come through the Luminant generation subsidiary — Vistra's Texas-based fossil and nuclear generation operating company — where she served as VP and General Counsel before elevation to the corporate role. Her practice background at Gardere Wynne Sewell encompassed corporate and securities work alongside trial practice, a combination relevant to a company that operates in contested regulatory environments and whose commercial positions in wholesale markets generate ongoing counterparty and regulatory litigation exposure.

Scott Hudson leads the retail operation as President of Vistra Retail, overseeing TXU Energy and the company's competitive retail portfolio across sixteen states. Hudson's background is non-traditional: he trained as a commercial lawyer at Troutman Sanders before roles at MBNA America, ChoicePoint, and LexisNexis — businesses built on customer identification, data analytics, and credit risk — before joining TXU Energy in 2011. The analytical toolkit for a competitive retail electricity business is closer to financial services than to generation operations: customer acquisition cost optimisation, lifetime-value modelling, churn prediction, and price-to-beat positioning in a market with real-time switching. Hudson's background aligns that toolkit directly.

The government affairs function is led by Sano Blocker, SVP of Government Affairs, who has been with the company and its predecessor entities since 2008, holding the equivalent role at Energy Future Holdings before carrying it through the bankruptcy emergence into the Vistra structure. His continuity through the EFH restructuring and the post-emergence period builds an institutional memory of legislative and regulatory dynamics — at the PUCT, the Texas Legislature, the NRC, and in Washington on IRA implementation — that an externally recruited government affairs head would require years to replicate.

## Nuclear governance: Vistra Vision and the Energy Harbor inheritance

Vistra Vision, the subsidiary established to hold the company's nuclear generation assets, carries dual institutional lineage: the legacy Comanche Peak operations team built under TXU and then Vistra ownership in Glen Rose, Texas, and the Energy Harbor nuclear organisation that operated Davis-Besse and Perry in Ohio and Beaver Valley 1 and 2 in Pennsylvania. The board-level governance of the nuclear business is anchored by John W. ("Bill") Pitesa, who joined the Vistra board in 2024 concurrent with the March Energy Harbor acquisition closing and chairs the board's Generation and Safety Oversight Committee.

Pitesa's career in the nuclear industry spans more than forty years: he served as Chief Nuclear Officer at Duke Energy — one of the largest nuclear operators in the United States — before serving as Chief Nuclear Officer of the Nuclear Energy Institute, the same trade body on whose board Jim Burke sits as a current member. Before the acquisition closed, Pitesa had chaired the nuclear safety and oversight committee of Energy Harbor's own board. His appointment to the Vistra board at the moment of the acquisition's closing was a deliberate governance decision: it brought the Energy Harbor nuclear committee chair directly into the combined entity's board-level nuclear oversight structure, providing continuity of safety governance through what is always a challenging integration period for nuclear operations.

## The board: post-bankruptcy composition calibrated for merchant power

Scott Helm has chaired the Vistra board since 2017. His career began at Goldman Sachs in fixed income and investment banking before he became EVP and Chief Financial Officer of Orion Power Holdings, a merchant power generator active in the competitive-market build-out of the early 2000s. He was subsequently a founding partner of Energy Capital Partners, the energy-focused private equity firm. The ECP founding role is the thread that explains his Chairmanship: Energy Capital Partners was a significant participant in the EFH restructuring and Vistra's emergence from Chapter 11, and Helm's position as Chairman reflects the governance continuity from that creditor-to-equity-holder transition.

Gavin Baiera has been on the board since 2016 — the bankruptcy emergence year itself — as Senior Managing Director and Partner at Centerbridge Partners, the multi-strategy private investment firm that was among the distressed-credit holders of EFH and TCEH debt through the restructuring. Baiera previously ran Strategic Finance at Morgan Stanley and was a Managing Director at Angelo, Gordon and Co., making him a structurally sophisticated voice on Vistra's capital structure, hedging programme, and capital allocation decisions.

Paul Barbas joined in 2018 through the Dynegy acquisition, which brought Dynegy's independent directors into the combined company's board. He is a former President and CEO of DPL Inc., the holding company for Ohio utility Dayton Power and Light, and held EVP-level operating roles at Chesapeake Utilities and Allegheny Power. J.R. Sult, also a Dynegy-acquisition director and the Audit Committee chair since 2018, is a career CFO: EVP and CFO of Marathon Oil, EVP and CFO of El Paso Corporation, VP and Controller at Halliburton Energy Services, and earlier an audit partner at Arthur Andersen. The Dynegy pair provides peer-utility operating challenge and financial-reporting-grade audit governance simultaneously.

Lisa Crutchfield chairs the Social Responsibility and Compensation Committee and brings regulatory authority experience that is rare at the board level: she served as Vice Chairman of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission in the early 1990s before senior executive roles at National Grid as EVP and Chief Regulatory, Risk and Compliance Officer, at PECO (an Exelon subsidiary) as SVP of Regulatory Affairs, and at Duke Energy as VP of Energy Policy. The PJM-geography regulatory depth — Pennsylvania in particular — maps directly onto the Energy Harbor nuclear assets operating within PJM's footprint.

Hilary Ackermann chairs the Sustainability and Risk Committee. Her final role at Goldman Sachs was as Chief Risk Officer of Goldman Sachs Bank USA, overseeing the bank's market, credit, and counterparty risk frameworks. That formation — systematic quantification of commodity price exposure, counterparty default risk, and tail risk — maps onto the principal financial risk the Vistra equity story carries: unhedged power price volatility in ERCOT and PJM is the variable that drives the equity return over any given twelve-month period.

Julie Lagacy has chaired the Nominating and Governance Committee since 2023. She spent the bulk of her career at Caterpillar across finance, HR, global information services (as CIO), and enterprise strategy, ending as Chief Sustainability and Strategy Officer. Her industrial-CFO background and cybersecurity governance training address the operational technology and information security risk exposure of a company running nuclear plants, gas-fired generation, and a large retail electricity trading platform under the same corporate roof.

Rob Walters joined the board in 2024 — again concurrent with the Energy Harbor closing — having retired from Gibson, Dunn and Crutcher in 2023 after serving on the firm's worldwide executive committee. Before his final chapter at Gibson Dunn, Walters had served as EVP and General Counsel of Energy Future Holdings Corp. His presence provides what no external director search could manufacture: institutional memory of the EFH structure, its regulatory history in Texas, and the commercial relationships that predated Vistra's 2016 emergence, combined with four decades of outside-counsel perspective on the electric power sector.

Arcilia Acosta has been on the board since 2020. She is CEO of CARCON Industries and Construction and founder and CEO of Southwestern Testing Laboratories, both Texas-based enterprises. She served on the Energy Future Holdings board for a decade, providing predecessor-entity governance continuity, and chaired the Dallas Citizens Council in 2023 and 2024. Her Texas civic and business presence is relevant to the regulatory and community relations dimensions of the company's continued ERCOT presence.

The resulting composition — a Goldman-and-ECP founding partner as Chairman, a Centerbridge distressed-credit investor as the longest-tenured independent director, two Dynegy-acquisition executives providing utility-CEO and CFO-grade challenge, a forty-year nuclear industry veteran anchoring nuclear safety governance, a former Pennsylvania PUC regulator overseeing compensation, a Goldman risk officer overseeing commodity risk, and a former EFH General Counsel providing predecessor-entity institutional memory — is explicitly calibrated for the post-bankruptcy merchant-power-plus-competitive-retail operating model Vistra runs. It is not the board of a regulated utility with a guaranteed rate of return. It is the board of a company whose equity return is shaped, quarter by quarter, by the price of power at the ERCOT North hub at peak demand hours and by the PJM capacity market's willingness to price scarcity.

chapters.title: Microsoft, hyperscalers, TXU retail customers, and the gas-and-uranium supply chain
chapters.body:
## The Hyperscaler Turn

When Jim Burke stepped back to assess Vistra's 2024 results in the company's February 2025 earnings release, he reached for a phrase that would have seemed grandiose just three years earlier: "a transformational year." The substance behind it was hard to argue. Vistra had closed on Energy Harbor, renewed Comanche Peak's operating licence through 2053, joined the S&P 500, and secured two large power purchase agreements with two of the world's most creditworthy corporate counterparties.

> "We've started construction on two new solar facilities, a 200 MW site backed by Amazon in Texas and a 405 MW site backed by Microsoft in Illinois."
> — Jim Burke, Q2 2024 earnings call, August 8, 2024

Those two sentences, tucked into an already eventful earnings release, marked Vistra's formal entry into the hyperscaler offtake business. The Microsoft deal — a long-term PPA for a 405 MW solar facility under development in Illinois — and the companion Amazon agreement for a 200 MW Texas solar project together totalled more than 600 MW of new contracted renewable capacity. Construction was under way on both as of Q1 2025. No strike price or contract duration was disclosed in SEC filings.

The solar agreements reflect the immediate contracting posture available in 2024: hyperscalers seeking to match their data-centre load growth with new clean electrons are constrained by what can be permitted, financed, and constructed within multi-year capital cycles. Utility-scale solar on previously coal-impacted land — Vistra has been converting retired Illinois coal plant sites under that state's Coal-to-Solar Initiative — offers speed and regulatory clarity that nuclear repowering, however commercially attractive, cannot match on the same timeline. But the solar PPAs are arguably a staging post, not the destination, for a company that now operates the second-largest competitive nuclear fleet in the United States.

## A 6.4 GW Nuclear Fleet and Its Hyperscaler Potential

Vistra's nuclear portfolio — 2.4 GW Comanche Peak in Texas plus the four Energy Harbor reactors in Ohio and Pennsylvania totalling roughly 4 GW — generates electricity with a capacity factor consistently above 90 percent. For hyperscalers, that profile is as close to purpose-built power as the grid offers: always-on, carbon-free, not contingent on weather. The IRA's Section 45U production tax credit, which provides a floor on nuclear economics through a sliding-scale PTC tied to the prevailing power price, has further de-risked the assets and made long-term offtake pricing more tractable.

On the Q3 2024 earnings call, Burke indicated Vistra was "making progress" on plans to develop up to 2,000 MW of new dispatchable natural gas generation in ERCOT, conditional on market reform implementation and forward price trajectory. That framing — evaluating regulatory catalysts before committing capital — extends to nuclear offtake as well. On multiple earnings calls through 2024 and into 2025, the team signalled active discussions with additional hyperscalers about the nuclear fleet, without announcing specific counterparties or terms.

The Comanche Peak licence renewal, approved by the NRC through 2050 and 2053 for units 1 and 2 respectively, removed a material uncertainty from any prospective long-term nuclear PPA. A 20-year PPA anchored to a plant whose operating licence expires in 2025 is a difficult proposition; the same contract anchored to a plant licenced through mid-century is something a hyperscaler's treasury team can bring to its board.

## TXU Energy: The Retail Anchor

Against this forward-looking hyperscaler narrative sits a business that has generated cash for over two decades: TXU Energy, Vistra's Texas retail brand and the largest competitive electricity retailer in the state. TXU serves approximately five million residential and business customers across the ERCOT footprint, competing in a fully deregulated market where switching is permitted and price discovery is real.

The retail segment generated $1,463 million in adjusted EBITDA for fiscal year 2024, up from $1,105 million in 2023 — a 32 percent increase reflecting both volume growth and improved margin management. The second quarter of 2024 was particularly striking: retail EBITDA reached $789 million in a single quarter, a figure Burke described as representing "retail performance levels not achieved in the more than two decades competitive markets have been open." In a year when the Texas wholesale market delivered its share of volatility, the ability of the integrated retail book to capture margin on that volatility — buying and selling around the TXU customer load — was the structural hedge working exactly as designed.

Vistra also operates Ambit Energy, the multi-state retail electricity and natural gas brand acquired in 2019, which extends competitive supply to customers in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, New York, and other deregulated states. The Energy Harbor acquisition added approximately one million additional retail customers in PJM markets, predominantly in Ohio and Pennsylvania, deepening the retail book outside Texas for the first time at scale. Retail EBITDA from the East segment, which houses Energy Harbor's contribution, reached $2,017 million in fiscal 2024 — effectively matching the Texas segment's $2,032 million, reflecting the transformation in Vistra's geographic earnings mix.

## Wholesale Market Exposure

The remainder of Vistra's generation output sells through the five ISO/RTO markets where it operates: ERCOT, PJM, MISO, NYISO, and ISO-NE. Each market has its own capacity construct, energy price formation mechanism, and ancillary services stack, and Vistra manages a sophisticated commercial hedging programme across all of them.

The hedging posture has been consistently aggressive: as of the Q3 2024 earnings call, Vistra was approximately 100 percent hedged for the balance of 2024, roughly 96 percent for 2025, and around 64 percent for 2026. By the February 2025 full-year release, the company reported approximately 80 percent hedge coverage for 2026 and reaffirmed 2025 guidance of $5.5 billion to $6.1 billion adjusted EBITDA from ongoing operations. PJM's 2025/26 capacity auction, which cleared at dramatically elevated prices in July 2024 — reflecting genuine capacity scarcity in the mid-Atlantic and Great Lakes region — materially improved the revenue outlook for Energy Harbor's Ohio and Pennsylvania fleet.

## Natural Gas: Flexible Backbone and Supply Chain

Natural gas-fired generation accounts for the largest share of Vistra's installed capacity, roughly 28 GW or more of the approximately 41 GW fleet. The gas book spans combined-cycle plants optimised for baseload-adjacent running and simple-cycle peakers designed to capture scarcity pricing during demand spikes. In ERCOT, where there is no capacity market and generators earn revenue solely through energy and ancillary service prices, peaker margin is highly correlated with weather extremes.

Natural gas supply is contracted through a combination of Henry Hub-indexed physical supply agreements and regional basis hedges, with pipeline transportation agreements covering delivery to individual plant gates. Vistra does not operate upstream gas assets, making it a price-taker at Henry Hub and at regional basis differentials — a structure that keeps the balance sheet clean but leaves earnings exposed to regional gas price dislocations, particularly the Waha Hub basis blow-outs that have periodically flipped west Texas gas prices negative.

Vistra's response to the structural demand signal from ERCOT — AI data centre load, electrification of industrial processes, and population growth — has been a stated commitment to add up to 2,000 MW of new dispatchable gas in Texas, contingent on PUCT market reforms providing sufficient investment signals. In May 2025, Vistra moved decisively in the broader merchant gas market with a separate transaction: a $1.9 billion agreement to acquire approximately 2,600 MW of modern combined-cycle and combustion turbine capacity from Lotus Infrastructure Partners, spanning PJM, New England, New York, and California.

> "We believe natural gas fired generation will continue to play an ever-increasing role in the reliability, affordability, and flexibility of U.S. power grids for years to come."
> — Jim Burke, May 2025

The Lotus deal, priced at approximately $743 per kilowatt and implying roughly seven times 2026 adjusted EBITDA, extended Vistra's gas presence into markets where it had previously been modest, deepening the multi-ISO earnings diversification the Energy Harbor acquisition began.

## The Uranium Supply Chain

For a merchant generator, nuclear fuel cycle supply chain management is among the most operationally consequential tasks that never appears on a headline earnings slide. Vistra's 6.4 GW nuclear fleet requires a continuous pipeline of uranium concentrate, conversion services, enrichment, and fuel fabrication — each representing a distinct supply market with its own geopolitical exposure.

Westinghouse Electric, the dominant Western nuclear services firm, is the principal fuel fabricator for Vistra's pressurised water reactor fleet, which includes Comanche Peak, Davis-Besse, and Beaver Valley. Perry, a boiling water reactor, draws on the GE Hitachi supply chain. Uranium concentrate is sourced through long-term contracts with producers in Kazakhstan, Canada, and Australia, reflecting a diversified procurement posture designed to reduce exposure to any single jurisdiction. Conversion — the step that transforms U₃O₈ into uranium hexafluoride — is bottlenecked globally by a limited number of facilities, principally ConverDyn (US), Cameco (Canada), and Orano (France), making that segment of the supply chain a particular focus for multi-year contracting.

The IRA's Section 45U production tax credit, active from 2024, effectively places a floor under nuclear economics in years when wholesale power prices fall below roughly $43 per MWh (adjusted for inflation). That floor has reduced the urgency of locking every megawatt-hour into a long-term PPA at whatever price the market offers in a given month — providing Vistra's nuclear commercial team the optionality to hold out for hyperscaler-grade contract structures that reflect the genuine scarcity value of always-on zero-carbon capacity.

Coal supply, once a major procurement consideration for Vistra's legacy Illinois and Ohio plants, has diminished substantially as the coal retirement programme advances. The Illinois Coal-to-Solar conversions at Baldwin and Coffeen — which brought 70 MW and 46 MW of solar-plus-storage online in 2024 — are the visible expression of that transition, converting stranded land and grid interconnection rights into renewable generation infrastructure that can support new offtake agreements.

chapters.title: Where Vistra sits against Constellation, NRG, NextEra, and Talen
chapters.body:
## A Market Reshaped

The January 2025 close of Constellation Energy's acquisition of Calpine Corporation redrew the competitive map of US merchant power in a single stroke. In its wake, Vistra Corp emerged as the clear number two in the US independent power producer hierarchy — a position it had been building toward since its own emergence from the Energy Future Holdings Chapter 11 in October 2016 and accelerated decisively through the March 2024 Energy Harbor acquisition. Standing second in a two-player tier was a materially different strategic position than the ranking alone implied. The competitive moat Vistra had carved — deep ERCOT penetration, retail integration through TXU Energy, and a first-mover advantage in the hyperscaler nuclear PPA market — distinguished it from a peer group that ranged from Constellation's nuclear behemoth to NRG Energy's multi-market competitive supply business to Talen Energy's smaller-scaled but historically significant nuclear play.

## Constellation: The Nuclear Benchmark

No peer comparison begins honestly without a clear-eyed accounting of the scale gap between Vistra and its principal comparable. Before absorbing Calpine, [Constellation Energy](https://investor.constellationenergy.com) operated approximately 22 gigawatts of nuclear capacity — the largest nuclear fleet in the United States and roughly 3.4 times Vistra's post-Energy-Harbor portfolio of 6.4 gigawatts. The Calpine deal added approximately 27 gigawatts of gas-fired and geothermal capacity, pushing Constellation's pro-forma installed base to approximately 49 gigawatts against Vistra's approximately 41 gigawatts as of the frozen window. By that arithmetic, Constellation commanded roughly 19 percent more total capacity than Vistra, and its nuclear advantage was wider still in proportional terms.

| Company | Total Capacity (approx.) | Nuclear (approx.) | Principal Market Anchor | Retail Presence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Constellation (post-Calpine pro-forma) | ~49 GW | ~22 GW | PJM | Constellation New Energy |
| Vistra (post-Energy Harbor) | ~41 GW | ~6.4 GW | ERCOT + PJM | TXU Energy, ~5M customers |
| NRG Energy | Multi-market | Minimal | ERCOT + multi-market | Reliant / NRG Retail |
| Talen Energy | Smaller-scaled | ~2.5 GW | PJM | None (wholesale) |
| NextEra Energy | ~70+ GW (incl. regulated) | Limited merchant nuclear | Florida + US renewables | FPL (regulated) |

The nuclear gap was the more consequential differential. Constellation's 22 GW offered large-volume, multi-site PJM capacity that Vistra's 6.4 GW could not yet match on pure megawatt terms. Constellation's September 2024 TMI-Microsoft deal became the reference transaction for nuclear-hyperscaler PPAs — but Vistra executed first, in May 2024, demonstrating PPA execution capability that the four-month precedence signalled to investors. The IRA Section 45U floor applied to both fleets, with Constellation's larger absolute benefit.

## Talen Energy: The Template That Made It Possible

Before either Vistra or Constellation had signed a hyperscaler-nuclear PPA, Talen Energy had already demonstrated that the structure was commercially viable. In March 2024, Talen — a smaller-scaled merchant generator that had emerged from Chapter 11 in May 2023 — announced an arrangement with Amazon Web Services for a data centre campus to be located adjacent to the Susquehanna nuclear generating station in Pennsylvania. The Cumulus Data campus arrangement was structurally distinct from a traditional wholesale PPA — it was a colocation model giving AWS direct access to on-site nuclear generation — but it served as proof-of-concept that hyperscalers would pay for proximity to firm, carbon-free baseload capacity.

Talen's Susquehanna plant, at approximately 2.5 gigawatts, was the company's principal nuclear asset and the principal draw for AWS. Talen did not have the retail integration, the multi-market generation footprint, or the gas-fired hedging capacity that Vistra or Constellation could bring to a hyperscaler negotiation. Its transaction was structurally innovative but commercially circumscribed by scale. What it provided — to Vistra, to Constellation, and to the market as a whole — was a working template. Within two months of the Talen-AWS announcement, Vistra had signed the Microsoft Comanche Peak PPA. Within six months, Constellation had announced the TMI deal. The March-to-September 2024 sequence established Talen as the architect of a market segment that its two larger competitors moved swiftly to occupy.

## NRG Energy: Competitive Supply Without the Nuclear Leg

NRG Energy occupied a structurally distinct position in the merchant power hierarchy. With a multi-market generation portfolio spanning ERCOT, PJM, and other US markets, NRG was a scaled competitive supply business with a meaningful retail operation — Reliant Energy in Texas and NRG-branded retail in other deregulated markets. But NRG had substantially exited its nuclear exposure in earlier years, leaving it without the always-on, carbon-free generation that the AI hyperscaler demand cycle was rewarding at a premium in both bilateral PPA pricing and equity valuation multiples.

NRG's ERCOT footprint gave it exposure to Texas power price volatility, but not at the scale or integration depth of Vistra's combined generation and TXU retail position. Where Vistra could structurally hedge ERCOT generation risk through a retail book of approximately five million Texas customers — with generation revenues partially offset by retail customer demand — NRG's Texas retail operation was smaller and its generation-to-retail matching less complete. NRG was a legitimate competitive supply business; it was not a nuclear play, and in the 2024-to-2026 environment, that distinction was being priced materially by equity markets.

## NextEra Energy: Scale at a Different Altitude

NextEra Energy was not a direct merchant power comparable to Vistra, but its competitive relevance shaped the broader investor context for the sector. Florida Power & Light, NextEra's regulated utility, served millions of Florida customers under a cost-of-service regulatory compact — a fundamentally different business model from Vistra's unhedged merchant risk exposure. [NextEra Energy Resources](https://www.nexteraenergyresources.com), the unregulated subsidiary, was the largest US renewables developer by installed capacity, with wind and solar assets across dozens of states. Total NextEra capacity — regulated and unregulated combined — exceeded 70 gigawatts, making it the largest US electric utility by generation footprint.

The strategic question NextEra posed for Vistra investors was whether the AI data centre power demand cycle would disproportionately reward nuclear and dispatchable gas — Vistra's core commercial proposition — or whether a longer-duration buildout of renewables and storage would erode that premium over subsequent years. NextEra had nuclear exposure through its Florida Power & Light interests, but these were proportionally small against its dominant renewables franchise. Through the frozen window, NextEra's renewables-weighted profile had not attracted the same equity re-rating that nuclear-anchored merchants received.

## The Texas Structural Advantage

The dimension of Vistra's competitive positioning that most resisted simple peer comparison was its ERCOT anchor. No other scaled US IPP — not Constellation, not NRG, not Talen — had the same depth of operational integration into the Texas power system. [Vistra](https://investor.vistracorp.com) operated approximately 22 gigawatts of generation within ERCOT, making it the largest single merchant operator in that market. The TXU Energy retail franchise, serving approximately five million Texas residential and business customers, provided a natural demand-side hedge against ERCOT wholesale price volatility that vertically integrated utilities took for granted but that most merchant generators could not replicate.

ERCOT's structural dynamics had become among the most investor-relevant in US power by the mid-2020s. Texas attracted a disproportionate share of new AI data centre development — driven by land availability, permitting speed relative to other jurisdictions, and a deregulated power market that allowed large commercial and industrial customers to negotiate directly with generators outside the traditional utility tariff framework. The ERCOT reserve margin tightened through the mid-2020s as demand growth from data centres, manufacturing reshoring, and electrification outpaced new supply additions, and the resulting capacity scarcity was a principal driver of the Vistra equity re-rating. Constellation and NRG each had ERCOT exposure, but neither could claim Texas as a defining strategic axis with the same depth that Vistra could.

## The Merchant Hierarchy at the Frozen Window
